1000976.etyen:
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian Kȍsovo, originally an ellipsis of Serbo-Croatian Kosovo polje (“Blackbird Field”). The element Kosovo is the neuter singular of a possessive adjective formed from kos (“blackbird”) with the possessive suffix -ov, agreeing with polje (“field”). The name therefore literally means “blackbird's field”, or more idiomatically “field of blackbirds”.
Compare the parallel borrowings Danish Kosovo, Swedish Kosovo, German Kosovo, Dutch Kosovo, Finnish Kosovo and Czech Kosovo.

en.g: a male given name from Medieval Latin [in turn from Old Persian], equivalent to English Caspar

1001232.etyen:
An older spelling variant of Kaspar and Kasper, continuing Medieval Latin Caspar. The name was traditionally assigned to one of the Magi in Western Christianity, although the Magi are not named in the biblical text itself. It is usually explained as ultimately deriving from an Old Persian title meaning “treasurer”, but the precise route into the medieval personal name is uncertain.
The spelling Caspar has a longstanding Norwegian tradition, with bearers in Norwegian and Danish–Norwegian society from at least the seventeenth century.
Compare Danish Caspar, Swedish Caspar, German Caspar, Dutch C

Borrowed from French appareil (“equipment, gear”), a deverbal of French appareiller (“to prepare, equip”), from Middle French appareiller (“to equip, make ready”), from Old French apareillier (“to prepare, equip”), from Vulgar Latin Vulgar Latin *appariculāre (“to equip, prepare”), from Latin apparō (“to prepare, make ready, equip”). The former continues Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”), while parō ultimately derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *perh₃- (“to provide, produce”).
